title: SYSK’s Summer Movie Playlist: Josh and Chuck's List of Horror Movies that Changed the Genre
summary: Josh and Chuck count down horror movies that changed the genre, drawn from a Grabster (Grabster's list on HowStuffWorks) article and expanded with additional picks. The episode is a playlist rerun from 2017, reposted in June 2025. They cover The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari (1920) and German expressionism, Blood Feast (1963) and gore, Night of the Living Dead (1968) and the modern zombie, The Exorcist (1973), Jaws (1975) and the summer blockbuster release, Halloween (1978) and the slasher genre, The Blair Witch Project (1999) and found footage, Scream (1996) and meta horror, and Psycho (1960). They close with a listener mail item from Eric about Gen X nostalgia and Schoolhouse Rock.

segments.title: Opening banter and episode setup
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck banter, introduce the episode as a list of horror films that changed the genre, and frame it as a Grabster-inspired list with additions.
topics: horror movies that changed the genre

segments.title: Horror talk and Toby's movie The Ghost Story
segments.summary: Josh plugs a film produced by his friend Toby, The Ghost Story, released by A24. They discuss recent A24 horror films including The Witch, The Blackcoat's Daughter, and It Comes at Night, and the state of modern horror.

segments.title: The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari and German expressionism
segments.summary: The 1920 German film is called the first horror movie. Its surreal sets, angled staircases, and shadows, and its roots in post-World War One German expressionism, established using the set to create a creepy mood. The hypnotist-and-sleepwalker plot is discussed.

segments.title: Blood Feast and on-screen gore
segments.summary: Herschell Gordon Lewis and David F. Friedman made Blood Feast (1963) on a fourteen-page outline, shot cheaply in Miami, and showed gore such as brains, entrails, and dismemberment that films had not shown before. It was a financial success and inspired special effects artists like Tom Savini. The Grand Guignol theater in Paris is mentioned as a precursor.

segments.title: Night of the Living Dead and the modern zombie
segments.summary: George Romero's 1968 film, shot in black and white in Pittsburgh on a small budget, created the modern flesh-eating zombie and cast a Black lead for lack of a reason beyond merit. Roger Ebert's 1969 review describes a matinee of children whose mood changed as the film went on. Critics read Vietnam and family collapse into it, and Romero killed off his hero at the end.

segments.title: The Exorcist and the demonic possession subgenre
segments.summary: William Peter Blatty's 1971 novel was adapted into The Exorcist (1973) by William Friedkin. It spawned a demonic-possession subgenre, was nominated for Best Picture, sold millions of tickets, and drew pushback from religious leaders such as Billy Graham. The film's intergenerational conflict theme is discussed.

segments.title: Jaws and the summer blockbuster
segments.summary: Jaws is praised by Chuck, who calls it a near-perfect film. Spielberg's shoot ran long and over budget, the mechanical shark (nicknamed Bruce) often failed, and the film's wide release on about 435 screens and heavy marketing created the summer blockbuster model. Chuck argues it is more adventure than horror.

segments.title: Halloween and the slasher genre
segments.summary: John Carpenter's Halloween (1978), shot in about twenty days, with Jamie Lee Curtis and the Michael Myers mask (a painted Captain Kirk mask), established the slasher genre's faceless, relentless, walking killer. Earlier slashers like Black Christmas are mentioned. It grossed about forty-seven million domestic.

segments.title: The Blair Witch Project and found footage
segments.summary: The Blair Witch Project (1998) is credited with establishing the found footage genre, helped by an early viral website and a rumor it was real. Its directors, Eduardo Sanchez and Daniel Myrick, shot it in eight days. Earlier films such as Mondo Cane and Cannibal Holocaust used documentary-style footage.

segments.title: Scream and meta horror
segments.summary: Scream (1996), written by Kevin Williamson and directed by Wes Craven, was a box-office hit that popularized meta horror, which references horror tropes. The original title was Scary Movie Number Two. Drew Barrymore's early death, the mask choice, and casting are discussed. Related meta films Tucker and Dale vs Evil, Zombieland, and Cabin in the Woods are mentioned.

segments.title: Psycho and Hitchcock's twist
segments.summary: Hitchcock's Psycho (1960), based loosely on Ed Gein, killed its lead character halfway through, breaking audience expectations and showing that the monster was already on screen. The Bates house and the shower scene are discussed. Owen Gleiberman's analysis is cited. Anthony Hopkins and Toby Jones Hitchcock films are mentioned. A listener note corrects a claim about Anthony Perkins directing The Blackcoat's Daughter.

segments.title: Wrap-up of horror list
segments.summary: Hosts encourage listeners to watch horror films and check the Grabster list on HowStuffWorks.

segments.title: Listener mail: Eric on Schoolhouse Rock and Gen X nostalgia
segments.summary: Listener Eric proposes that Gen X nostalgia comes mainly from pop culture and child-targeted marketing of the seventies and eighties, not from Schoolhouse Rock. Josh and Chuck respond.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts ask for listener theories and give contact and website details.
